scores.evidence: True zero write-pause needs two-way replication with conflict handling. I don't recommend it for scheduling, because conflicts here mean two patients in one slot.
scores.rationale: Technical claims about CDC replication, read-only promotion, lag draining to zero, DNS TTL, and the real limits of 'zero downtime' are all accurate, including the subtle areas.

scores.evidence: Writes pause for under 60 seconds at cutover, during the quietest hour. The app queues or retries them
scores.rationale: Resolves the 'no downtime' ambiguity explicitly and sensibly, covers all implied core needs (compliance, interfaces, cutover, rollback), and is credibly buildable with explicit deferrals.

scores.evidence: Writes go to one database only; brief write freeze
scores.rationale: Single-write-authority decision is honored consistently from design through runbook to rollback; phases, data flows, and interface routing connect without contradiction.

scores.evidence: Rehearse the full cutover and rollback at least twice in a staging environment, and time each step.
scores.rationale: Validation targets the actual risks (reconciliation checksums, lag=0 gate, 1.5x peak load, AZ/network failover, rehearsed rollback) with checkable criteria and continues post-cutover via daily reconciliation and dashboards.

scores.evidence: I don't know your specific system, so I've made some assumptions. They're listed at the end along with the questions that would most change this plan.
scores.rationale: Assumptions are explicit, reasonable, and ranked by which would change the design; estimates like the 5-8 month timeline are clearly labeled as rough.

scores.evidence: A hidden integration breaks (an old IP address or hostname nobody knew about) | Capture network traffic during discovery; monitor the interface engine
scores.rationale: Major domain failures (double-booking, hidden interfaces, latency, vendor refusal, compliance gaps) have concrete detection and mitigation, but subtler cases like duplicate writes when draining the queue or replication corruption handling are thin.

scores.evidence: IT staff on site at scheduling centers, dashboards for errors, response time, and HL7 queue depth.
scores.rationale: Deployment (IaC), rollback, meaningful health signals, command center, and hypercare are concrete, but steady-state incident ownership, access administration, and break-glass procedures are not addressed.

scores.evidence: Licensing limits. Some vendors restrict cloud hosting or require their approval.
scores.rationale: Beyond vendor licensing and a rough timeline, cloud run costs (Direct Connect, managed database, dual-running both environments for 30-90 days) and engineering cost drivers are ignored.

scores.evidence: Start reverse replication cloud -> on-prem, which keeps rollback possible
scores.rationale: The hard-to-reverse moments (cutover, decommission) get explicit reversal paths and gated timing, re-architecture is deliberately deferred, and the warm-standby window delays the irreversible step.

scores.evidence: Rehost or lightly replatform first... don't change the code and the location at the same time.
scores.rationale: Simplest workable approach with every element (private link, multi-AZ, CDC, rehearsals) justified by the domain, and improvements explicitly deferred until after the move.

scores.evidence: T-0 | Put on-prem database in read-only; app queues writes | T+15s | Confirm replication lag = 0; run final checksum
scores.rationale: Phased build order with reasoning, a timed cutover runbook, explicit go/no-go and rollback triggers, and stated questions that would change course make this immediately actionable.

checklist.evidence: Business Associate Agreement (BAA) signed with the cloud provider. Use only services covered by it... encryption at rest and in transit, key management, audit logging
ADT... Scheduling messages (HL7 SIU) to the EHR, billing/eligibility... Set up the interface engine so it can send to either environment
Load an initial database copy, then turn on continuous change replication... Reconcile data every day: appointment counts per day, provider, and location, plus checksums
Put on-prem database in read-only; app queues writes... Writes go to one database only; brief write freeze
Rehearse the full cutover and rollback at least twice... Start reverse replication cloud -> on-prem, which keeps rollback possible
a dedicated private link (AWS Direct Connect or Azure ExpressRoute)... with a site-to-site VPN as backup. Test latency from every clinic site.
spread across multiple availability zones... set target recovery times and data-loss limits
Identity | Active Directory/LDAP, SSO, service accounts
Load tests: at least 1.5x historical peak... Send read-only traffic (reports, schedule viewing) to the cloud first.
target: 1-2am on a low-volume weekday... Freeze batch jobs; command center open... IT staff on site at scheduling centers
Get vendor approval in Phase 0... archive it according to your record-retention policy. Wipe disks securely, with certificates of destruction.

traps.evidence: Load an initial database copy, then turn on continuous change replication... Rehearse the full cutover and rollback at least twice
True zero write-pause needs two-way replication with conflict handling. I don't recommend it for scheduling
Signed BAA, risk assessment, logging in place before any real patient data moves
Integrations are where hospital migrations usually fail, so map all of them
Leave redesigning the application for after the move; don't change the code and the location at the same time.

note: An expert-grade migration plan that avoids every trap, with a correct single-write-authority cutover and rehearsed rollback; the only real weaknesses are absent cost analysis, thin identity/break-glass detail, and untested backup/restore.
